title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM)
text:
Following the Score Matching with Langevin Dynamics (SMLD), Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) (Ho, Jain, and Abbeel 2020) formulated a Diffusion Models (DMs) as two separate processes. The forward, or diffusion process was defined as a fixed Markov chain that increasingly adds noise to the original data \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), being described as: \[
q(\boldsymbol{x}_{1:T}\mid \boldsymbol{x}_0) = \prod_{t=1}^T q(\boldsymbol{x}_t\mid \boldsymbol{x}_{t-1}),
\tag{1}\] where \(T\in \mathbb N\) is the number of states in the chain. Each transition in this process can be expressed as: \[
q(\boldsymbol{x}_t\mid \boldsymbol{x}_{t-1}) = \mathcal N\left(\boldsymbol{x}_t\mid \sqrt{1-\beta_t}\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1}, \beta_t\boldsymbol{I}\right),
\tag{2}\] where \(\{\beta_i\}_{i=1}^T\) is a variance schedule. The diffusion process admits sampling any step in the chain directly from the original sample, with the following: \[
\boldsymbol x_t = \sqrt{\overline{\alpha}_t}\boldsymbol x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \overline{\alpha}_t} \boldsymbol \epsilon,
\tag{3}\] where \(\alpha_t = 1 - \beta_t\), \(\overline{\alpha}_t = \prod_{s=1}^t \alpha_s\) and \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim \mathcal N(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\boldsymbol{0}, \boldsymbol{I})\).
The reverse process is a Markov chain where the Gaussian transitions are learned via a parametrized Neural Network (NN). Starting \(\boldsymbol{x}_T\sim\mathcal N(\boldsymbol{x}_T\mid \boldsymbol{0}, \boldsymbol{I})\), the NN parametrized by \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) approximates the following chain: \[
p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\left(\boldsymbol{x}_{0:T}\right) = p(\boldsymbol x_T) \prod_{t=1}^T p_{\boldsymbol \theta}(\boldsymbol x_{t-1}\mid \boldsymbol x_t).
\tag{4}\] Each transition step is expressed as: \[
p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_{t}) = \mathcal N\left(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1}\mid  {\boldsymbol\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t), {\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t)\right).
\tag{5}\] That is, the DM learns the mean \({\boldsymbol\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t)\) and variance \({\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t)\) to reverse the noise from \(\boldsymbol{x}_{t}\) to \(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1}\). To achieve this, the model is conditioned on the time step \(t\).
The NN is trained to minimize the negative log likelihood of the data. Making some algebraic steps: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L(\boldsymbol{\theta}) &= \mathbb E\left[ -\log p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol{x}_0)\right] \leq \mathbb E_q\left[- \log\frac{p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol x_{0:T})}{q(\boldsymbol{x}_{1:T} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_0)}\right] \\
&= \mathbb E_q\left[- \log p(\boldsymbol{x}_T) - \sum_{t\geq 1} \log\frac{p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol x_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t)}{q(\boldsymbol{x}_{t} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_{t-1})}\right] \\
&= \mathbb E_q\left[- \log p(\boldsymbol{x}_T) - \log \frac{p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol x_{0} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_1)}{q(\boldsymbol{x}_{1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_{0})} - \sum_{t> 1}\log \frac{p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol x_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t)}{q(\boldsymbol{x}_{t} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_{t-1})}\right].
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}\] Applying Bayes’ Theorem to the forward Markov chain: \[
\begin{aligned}
    &= \mathbb E_q\left[- \log p(\boldsymbol{x}_T) - \log \frac{p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol x_{0} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_1)}{q(\boldsymbol{x}_{1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_{0})} - \sum_{t> 1}  \log  \frac{p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol x_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t)q(\boldsymbol x_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_0)}{q(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_{t}, \boldsymbol{x}_0) q(\boldsymbol{x}_{t} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_{0})} \right]  \\
    &= \mathbb E_q\left[- \log \frac{p(\boldsymbol{x}_T)}{q(\boldsymbol{x}_T \mid \boldsymbol{x}_0)} - \log p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol x_{0} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_1)- \sum_{t> 1}  \log  \frac{p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol x_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t)}{q(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_{t}, \boldsymbol{x}_0)}\right] \\
    &= \mathbb E_q\bigg[ \underbrace{D_{\text{KL}} \bigg(q(\boldsymbol{x}_T \mid \boldsymbol{x}_0) \parallel p(\boldsymbol{x}_T) \bigg)}_{\mathcal L_T} \underbrace{- \log p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol x_{0} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_1)}_{\mathcal L_0}  \\
    &\qquad \qquad \qquad + \sum_{t> 1} \underbrace{D_{\text{KL}} \bigg(q(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_{t}, \boldsymbol{x}_0) \parallel p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x} _t) \bigg)}_{\mathcal L_{t-1}}\bigg],
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}\] where \(D_{\text{KL}}\) is the Kullback-Leibler divergence. Note that by fixing the forward process, the term \(\mathcal L_T\) does not depend on \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) and can therefore be ignored. For the \(\mathcal L_{1:T-1}\) terms, the variance of the NN is fixed to \({\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t) = \sigma_t^2\boldsymbol{I} = \beta_t \boldsymbol{I}\).
With the variance fixed, the KL divergence in the \(\mathcal{L}_{t-1}\) terms compares two Gaussian distributions. This simplifies to the mean squared error between their means. The posterior \(q(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t, \boldsymbol{x}_0)\) is also a Gaussian, therefore, minimizing \(\mathcal{L}_{t-1}\) is equivalent to minimizing the difference between the true posterior mean \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_t\) and the NN’s predicted mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\): \[
\mathcal L_{t-1} = \mathbb E_q \left[ \frac{1}{2\sigma_t^2} \left\| \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_t(\boldsymbol{x}_t, \boldsymbol{x}_0) - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t) \right\|^2 \right] + C,
\tag{8}\] where \(C\) is a constant independent of \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\). With some reparametrization tricks, it is possible to show that these terms can be expressed as: \[
\mathcal L_{t-1} = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol{x}_0, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}} \left[ \frac{\beta_t^2}{2\sigma_t^2 \alpha_t (1 - \overline{\alpha}_t)} \left\| \boldsymbol{\epsilon} - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t) \right\|^2 \right],
\tag{9}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t)\) is the noise predicted by the NN. It was observed that ignoring the weighting term lead to better results. This results in the final simplified objective function used to train DDPMs: \[
\mathcal L(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbb E_{t, \boldsymbol{x}_0, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}} \left[ \left\| \boldsymbol{\epsilon} - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t) \right\|^2 \right].
\tag{10}\]
After training the NN \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\) to approximate the noise added to the data, the model can be used to generate new samples from the learned data distribution \(p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\). The reverse process begins by sampling pure Gaussian noise \(\boldsymbol{x}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0}, \boldsymbol{I})\) and iteratively denoising it down to \(t=0\). The iterative process is described by: \[
\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left(\boldsymbol{x}_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\overline{\alpha}_t}} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t)\right) + \sigma_t\boldsymbol{z},
\tag{11}\] where \(\boldsymbol{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0}, \boldsymbol{I})\) for \(t > 1\). At the final step when \(t = 1\), \(\boldsymbol{z} = \boldsymbol{0}\) is set to output the deterministic mean, as adding noise at the very end would degrade the final image.

title: Cold-Diffusion (CD)
text:
Another diffusion paradigm is the Cold-Diffusion (CD) (Bansal et al. 2023) generalization. Although previous formulations specifically employed noise addition as the degradation scheme, CD showed that more general degradation operators could be used to train Diffusion Models (DMs).
Let \(\boldsymbol x_0\sim p_0\) be a data point and let \(\boldsymbol x_t = \boldsymbol D (\boldsymbol x_0, t)\) be the degradation of \(\boldsymbol x_0\) by the degradation operator \(\boldsymbol D\) at scale \(t\). Then, let \(\boldsymbol R_{\boldsymbol \theta}\) be the restoration operator that satisfies: \[
\boldsymbol R_{\boldsymbol \theta} \left(\boldsymbol D (\boldsymbol x_0, t), t\right) \approx \boldsymbol x_0.
\tag{1}\] That is, the restoration operator is a neural network parametrized by \(\boldsymbol \theta\). This network can be trained minimizing the following objective: \[
\mathcal L(\boldsymbol \theta) = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol x_0, t} \left\| \boldsymbol R_{\boldsymbol \theta} \left( \boldsymbol D(\boldsymbol x_0, t), t \right) - \boldsymbol x_0 \right\|,
\tag{2}\] where \(\boldsymbol x_0 \sim p_0\) and \(t\) is sampled from a degradation scale interval.
The CD formulation is particularly interesting for inverse problems, as the degradation and restoration operators can be directly employed during the DM training.

Code

Importing the packages.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter
from skimage import data
from skimage.transform import resize

Loading a data example.

x_0 = data.astronaut().astype(np.float32) / 255.0
num_steps = 5
timesteps = np.linspace(0, 1, num_steps)

Creating degradation schemes.

def degrade_blur(x, t, max_sigma=15.0):
    sigma = t * max_sigma
    if sigma == 0: return x
    return gaussian_filter(x, sigma=(sigma, sigma, 0))

def degrade_pixelate(x, t, min_res=4):
    if t == 0: return x
    h, w, c = x.shape

    curr_h = max(min_res, int(h * (1 - t) + min_res * t))
    curr_w = max(min_res, int(w * (1 - t) + min_res * t))

    downsampled = resize(x, (curr_h, curr_w), order=0, anti_aliasing=False)
    return resize(downsampled, (h, w), order=0, anti_aliasing=False)

def degrade_mask(x, t):
    if t == 0: return x
    h, w, c = x.shape
    mask_size_h = int(h * t)
    mask_size_w = int(w * t)

    start_y = (h - mask_size_h) // 2
    start_x = (w - mask_size_w) // 2

    x_t = x.copy()
    x_t[start_y:start_y+mask_size_h, start_x:start_x+mask_size_w, :] = 0.5
    return x_t

Plot the degradation schemes.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, num_steps, figsize=(12, 6))
plt.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.05, hspace=0.1)

for i, t in enumerate(timesteps):

    pix_t = degrade_pixelate(x_0, t)
    mask_t = degrade_mask(x_0, t)
